600/month).

Niche Down: (6:00 - 12:21) Recommends targeting a specific, high-value customer segment rather than the entire market to improve ad resonance.

Copy What Works: (12:23 - 15:37) Encourages using the Meta Ads Library to model successful creatives from competitors who have already tested their ads.

Focus on Direct Results: (15:38 - 18:05) Explains why you should prioritize sales or leads campaigns over awareness or traffic campaigns when operating on a small budget.

Leverage Organic Content: (18:06 - 19:59) Proposes using high-performing organic posts (like Instagram Reels) as free testing for future ad creative.

Adjust Acquisition Expectations: (20:15 - 25:50) Highlights the importance of understanding your customer lifetime value and being willing to spend appropriately to acquire customers rather than just chasing a high ROAS.

Consolidate Variables: (25:51 - 27:35) Advises simplifying your account structure (e.g., fewer ad sets) to consolidate data and help the Meta algorithm optimize faster.

But that's rare. By default, we're absolutely going to combine both cold and warm audiences into the same campaign and the same adset. So, the next thing we're trying to do with the new campaign structure is consolidate as much as possible. And that applies to both campaigns and adsets. We're going to try and run as few campaigns and as few adsets as possible. Often just using the one campaign and the one adset. I'll explain later on when we do and don't want to uh to do that. Why are we doing that? Well, it's best to combine the data into as few elements as possible. Let's say you generate 70 conversions in a week. Instead of having that spread across 10 different adsets, so seven conversions roughly per adset per week, Meta is going to struggle to optimize those adsets. Going to struggle to get out of the learning phase. Whereas, if that's in one adset, you're generating 70 conversions per week in that one adset. Meta is able to fully optimize. They're able to work out the best time of day to advertise, what ad impression frequency is required, advertise to this person instead of this person, use this ad instead of this ad. all the various points that Meta's system optimizes to get us more of what we want, more sales, more leads, whatever it is we've set up our campaign to optimize for, Meta can do that better with more conversion data. So much better to have that consolidated data into the one campaign, one adset as opposed to spread across lots of different elements that will struggle uh to optimize. Second reason why we want to consolidate is because we want to avoid auction overlap. Now, there's some misconceptions around overlap. A lot of people think I'm talking about audience overlap. When I say auction overlap, I'm not audience overlap would be you've got two different campaigns, two different adsets, and they're targeting a lot of the same audience. Now, that's not ideal, but the whole idea of that's going to increase the cost because you're bidding against yourself is a bit silly. There are thousands of advertisers trying to reach the same people. One extra campaign ad setting that not going to make much difference. But you can run into issues with auction overlap, which is a different thing. Meta systems are now very sophisticated at working out what ad impression frequency is required to get the outcome that you want. So Meta might work out, you know what, we're better off at generating four or five ad impressions for a single individual over a 24 48 hour time period as opposed to spreading out those ad impressions over a week. Well, Meta could plan that really well if it's just got the one campaign, one adset targeting a person, a group of people obviously, but we're talking about one individual user in this case, but targeting um a group of people. If you've got some ad impressions coming from one adset, some ad impressions coming from another adset or different campaigns, much more difficult for Meta to work out that delivery system of right, let's put an ad in front of this person four times over the next 48 hours. Much more difficult for them to be able to uh to do that. So, that's that's the issue that comes up with auction overlap. and you want to take advantage of what Meta's delivery system um is able to do. Okay. And how are we adapting to it with structure first. So, first off, the Andromeda algorithm has been a shift from audience to creative targeting. Now, what this very simply means is in the old algorithm, you would choose your audience, whether it's broad, interest, lookalikes, whatever, and the creatives you push into that ad set get targeted from that interest group. This has now flipped. Instead of an interest or a broad target deciding who the ads are going to be shown to, that has completely reversed. We now have a situation where whatever ads are within your ad set define the targeting on an individual level. This means that, yes, you could have completely different ads in the same ad set that target two very different people. It also means that you could have multiple ad sets in the same campaign targeting completely different people, even if the targeting, the interest group, or the broad is 100% the same. Now, I don't want to get too conceptual on this, but what this means is that your creative concepts matter more than ever. And the structure that we actually like to deploy to solve for Andromeda that we've proven out across 80-plus accounts at this point is one of with swim lanes. Now, swim lanes are a very simple philosophy that we need to separate prospecting, retargeting, and retention. So, the important part about swim lanes is that you as the advertiser actually know where you're spending your money. One of the biggest flaws that we see with Facebook is that it overspends on engage and existing customers. It's fine to spend a lot of money on engage. It's fine to spend a lot of money on existing customers. But what I don't like is when advertisers or brands that we work with think that they're spending money on prospects. They think they're spending money on new customers when in reality, they're actually spending a boatload of that cash on existing and engage, which they believe they're targeting in other places like email, SMS, and other retargeting methods. What we like to do is make sure that our swim lanes are clearly defined. Our first swim lane is prospecting. This is generally a CBO prospecting campaign mixed with a boatload of ad sets. Those could be a combination of broad and interest groups, even lookalikes if you'd like to give them a shot. The important part is that we're grouping a lot together in one campaign, and we are creating a hyper-competitive environment. I want to actually say that twice. A hyper-competitive environment is one of the most important things that you could have in a Facebook ads account because you're actually giving the algorithm some power to decide where to spend your money. Now, this is very, very different than a one campaign method or just throwing everything into one ad set because you could actually define minimum, maximum budgets and even put exclusions on things at the ad set level within your prospecting campaigns. That's the control, that's the levers that we like to have on our side without just giving all the power to Facebook. The second and third swim lanes are retargeting and retention. Retargeting is anyone who's visited your site and anyone who's engaged with your business. They know about you, very simple. Retention, on the other hand, is anyone who's purchased. This isn't someone who's added to cart. This isn't someone who almost purchased. They've handed you money. That is a very big difference between retargeting and retention. We want to make sure we're treating each of these buckets separately, we're dedicating our budget accordingly, and even in some cases curating the creative to each of these buckets. But most of the time, it's okay to have the same creatives in each with a big testing environment in our prospecting CBO. And you might ask, why? Why does this fix Andromeda? Why does this fix the issue that everyone seems to have in the back of their mind? It's actually quite simple. It starts in the prospecting CBO campaign. The prospecting CBO campaign now has the capability to spend its cash wherever it wants, meaning your audiences can individually be targeted per creative. So, think about it like this. If you separated all of your ad sets or all of your creative concepts into different campaigns, then you're controlling the budget. $200 here, $200 here, $200 here. But grouping these together, what it actually does is it allows you to still see very clearly with organized ad sets, set minimums and maximum budgets if you need, and with your total budget, so 200, 200, 200 equaling 600 on a total CBO budget, Facebook will distribute wherever the cash is best spent. And I know one issue that a lot of people have is that certain creatives don't get any spend. I'm here to tell you this is a feature, not a bug, most of the time. Not all the time. Most of the time, Facebook is saving you cash by doing this. So, what I would advise, if you really feel like there's an ad that you've put a lot of time or effort into, set a minimum budget, make sure it gets $25, $50 a day, let it ramp up a little bit. If it doesn't work after 7 days, kill that minimum budget. Okay, so our structures are complete. The second shift that I have seen and that basically everyone has seen because it actually happened. But now, targeting and really all the features are kind of coming back to us, which is a good thing. it comes to measurement, this is one of the places where we need to be accurate. And that accuracy has improved drastically with the introduction of incremental attribution. Now, I want to challenge all of these third-party attribution softwares because they do have their place, but I think people get too excited about them when we actually have the best tool natively built into Facebook. Think about it like this. Hyros, Triple Whale, and all third-party attribution platforms have only access to certain amounts of data. Imagine Facebook only had click-based data. The only signal that we were able to optimize on and the only algorithm input was click-based purchases. If that was the case and there was a third-party platform that came out that had the ability to see view purchases, click purchases, incremental purchases, and every engagement, every search, every like, favorite, comment, share that you've ever done over all time on your social platforms, I think everyone would pay boatloads of money for that third-party platform. And that is exactly what Meta is capable of doing with its standard attribution. It sounds so boring because it's built in, and there's fancy tools with great marketing slogans that actually sell us into programs that don't do as much as the actual Facebook tracking. And I don't want to discredit these tools because there are some use cases where they're great. But when it comes to measurement, the best measurement is Meta's measurement. And here's the hidden upside, the cross-channel effect. When you improve the quality of who you bring in and keep your traffic consistent, everything downstream gets better. Let's take a step back to look at what's really happening. Our creative testing upgrades the customer quality coming into the store. And because all spend runs through one system, Meta's Andromeda gets better at matching the right ad to the right buyer. And because we're not launching hundreds of random ads, all of our customers begin to look and feel and behave the same. Then we scale the budget to buy more of those higher quality customers. And all of that means that our site converts better, search and email pick up more revenue and even returning customer revenue also climbs. And that's the point. We're making the business better by buying better customers. That's why we judge success by the bank account, not just by platform ROAS. I don't really give a about ROAS. And this is the difference between optimizing ads like a performance marketer and being an operator scaling a business. I think about it like this, hunters versus farmers. Hunters lived in caves for 100,000 years living and dying by their ability to feed themselves today. Hunters measure success by ROAS and daily CPA. They ask, "Did this ad work today? What's my cost right now? Did it hit immediately?" They live and die by short-term swings. Once humanity learned how to farm, we went from living in caves to building empires and putting a man on the moon. We are in the empire building business. If you want to scale to the moon, you have to start thinking like a farmer. Farmers focus on feeding as many people as possible. One corn plant can produce three or four pounds of food and you can plant 10 other corn plants from what you don't eat. So for the same amount of work, over time you go from four pounds of food to 400 because you're focusing on building a better system and that's what farming is. Farmers focus on total profit and growth. Their job isn't to chase win after win, it's to build a system that works and to protect it and to scale it with the resources that system builds for itself. And that's what Andromeda one is actually optimizing for, similarity to produce scale. We're increasing the volume of high quality data flowing into the platform so it gets better at matching the right message to the right buyer and finding more of your best customers. Now, before you copy this structure, we have to talk about budget. Because a lower budget changes the rules just a little bit. If your budget isn't high enough to reliably get more than one ad set out of the learning phase, then everything lives in one ad set. Your control and your tests are just ads inside of the same ad set. Then you follow a simple ladder. One ad set until you can afford to get one testing and one control ad set. And then you scale until you can afford two testing ad sets. And even when I'm spending a million a month like I showed you before, I don't have more than two testing ad sets. Once you get there, you're done. You're ready to scale to the moon. So now that you understand what Andromeda one really is, it's not a tactic or a hack and it's definitely not a structure you copy and paste from a screenshot. It's a decision to stop being a hunter and to start being a farmer. It's choosing a system you can run every week, not a lucky ad you hope doesn't die. Now that you understand that, next we need to talk about the ad itself. I got to show you the exact ad format I use, how to build it and how to feed the algorithm the kind of data it needs to actually scale because the best structure in the world won't scale if your ads aren't teaching Meta to win and that is exactly what this next video is all about. >> [music]

Neither Harry and Kreacher like the agreement very much, since Harry though neither Harry and Kreacher like the arrangement, since Kreacher in the books played an indirect role in the death of Sirius while Kreacher made it clear that he wanted Bellatrix as his master instead of Harry. 

And Harry could not exactly give Kreacher clothes to free him because Kreacher, as a fiercely loyal pureblood house-elf, viewed his servitude as an honor rather than a burden, and would have despised the idea of freedom.

Not to mention that Kreacher held highly sensitive information about the Order of the Phoenix due to Grimauld Place being their base of operations. In other words, freeing him before Voldemort's defeat would have allowed Kreacher to run straight to the Malfoys and inform them of what the Order was doing

In the end, Kreacher remained at Grimauld Place, and it was proven that Harry was indeed his owner now when Harry ordered Kreacher to shut up when he started throwing a tantrum, with Kreacher being forced to obey (the house-elf then continued throwing a tantrum, but now silently).

  4. @patricioalanisvillarreal9616 [1 likes]: In the book, instead of picking Harry up at a subway, Dumbledore personally went to pick up Harry at the Dursley family house before taking him to the Burrow. 

But before they left, we got a very memorable scene where Dumbledore forced the Dursleys to sit down on a couch so he could talk to them (he even conjures four glasses of mead to offer them. And when they refuse, Dumbledore  uses a subtle bit of magic to make the glasses hover and gently nudge the sides of their heads until they comply).

Anyway, what makes this scene so cool is the way that Dumbledore firmly takes control of the whole event, shutting down Vernon Dursley's anger whenever he tries to speak up, and then harshly reprimanding the family for their years of cruel neglect and abuse towards harry.

You see, Dumbledore reminded Vernon and Petunia of the contents of the letter that he had placed besides baby Harry Potter when he had left him on the doorstep of the Dursley family sixteen years ago, after the first defeat of Voldemort and the deaths of Lily and James Potter. 

And even though the letter had specified that the Dursleys were to look after Harry and protect him in order to keep the love protection that Lily Potter had left on her son alive, the Dursleys flat out ignored the letter: instead of treating Harry like a nephew or a member of the family, they subjected him to cruelty and abuse.

In the end, about the only remotely positive thing that Dumbledore could say about the Dursleys and their dismal guardianship of Harry was that, at the very least, they avoided giving Harry the "appalling damage" they had inflicted upon Dudley, whom they had spoiled rotten by catering to his every whim (this in spite of the fact that Dudely was beginning to reform following the Dementor attack from last year).

After the severe cathartic scolding, Dumbledore then turns his attention to Harry, officially informs him of the inheritance he got from the late Sirius Black, before arranging for Harry to accompany him to the Burrow for the rest of the summer
  5. @patricioalanisvillarreal9616 [1 likes]: In this movie, Snape finally gets to teach Defense Against the Dark Arts, a positon he has wanted for a very long time in spite of his obvious talent and mastery of Potions.

Now, Dumbledore had always known Snape desired the job, and the main reason why he had denied him the positon was for two reasons.

The first being the fact that the job was jinxed to make a new teacher leave withn a year because of a spell that Voldemort had cast in the past, and Dumbledore did not want to potentially risk the life of Snape, someone he valued greatly. For his part, Harry hoped that Snape would die because of the jinx, but in the end, Snape ended up vacating the post not because he died, but because he fled Hogwarts after killing Dumbeldore)

The other reason being that Snape, as a former Death Eater, had a deep, historical fascination with the Dark Arts. Dumbledore also knew this and worried that placing Snape in that specific role would tempt him to return to the darkness

Now, since we did not get any scenes of Snape teaching the DADA in the movie, I am going to mention what he did do in the books:

In the books, Snape taught DADA by enforcing a strict, demanding curriculum that favored nonverbal spells, wandless defense, and combat and advanced spellwork. 

This was done because Snape believed in the advantages of nonverbal spell casting, emphasizing the split-second advantage it gives a duelist by not alerting the adversary to the magic and spell being performed when one said the name of the spell, and also forcing the students to rely on reflexes and silent concentration. This in turn resulted in Snape fiercely criticizing those who continued to speak out incantations like mere beginners.

As for Snape himself, he still remained the same severe, intimidating instructor in DADA that he was in Potons, constantly favoring his own Slytherin students while subjecting Gryffindors (like Harry) to harsh, relentless scrutiny. 

That being said, one could tell that Snape had a wholly different mood when he was teaching DADA compared to Potions, speaking of the Dark Arts in a way that resembled reverent fascination, viewing it as complex and sophisticated (my guess is that he was probably excited at finally getting the job and the subject matter he had always wanted).

As for Harry, while he initially struggled with nonverbal magic, he got a whole lot better after he started relying on the lessons he got from the copy of the Half-Blood Prince textbook. In fact, Harry even claimed at one point that the Half-Blood Prince was an even better teacher to him than Snape was (this only makes the reveal that Snape is the Half-Blood Prince all the funnier)
  6. @patricioalanisvillarreal9616 [1 likes]: In the books, there was also an ongoing subplot involving Fleur Delacour from book 4 that was ommitted for the movie.

You see, following the events of the Triwizard Tournament, during the summer of 1995, Fleur took a part-time job at Gringotts Wizarding Bank to improve her English, where she met William "Bill" Weasley, eldest child of the Weasley family, who was working there at Gringotts as well. 

The two were attracted to each other and started dating, eventually becoming engaged to be married. Meaning that when Book 6 starts, Fleur was already staying at the Weasley family home of The Burrow in the summer of 1996, so she could get to know Bill's family better before the wedding. 

Now, while Arthur, Ron, and Harry did not mind having Fleur at all at the house, Hermione, Ginny, and Molly Weasley did take issue, considering the French witch to be snooty, snobbish, and self-obsessed, with Ginny even taking to calling Fleur "Phlegm" due to her thick accent (the fact that Ron had an obvious crush on Fleur certainly did nothing to improve Hermione's mood).

As for Molly, she was the one who most disliked Fleur, mainly due to the latter constantly criticizing her house as well as her favourite singer, Celestina Warbeck. In particular, Molly believed that she and Fleur had absolutely nothing in common and that they had only gotten engaged in a hurry due to the dark times that they were living in.

Things came to a head after Dumbledore's death and the Battle at the Astronomy Tower, during which Bill Weasley (who had arrived at the school with a bunch of Aurors to protect the school alongside other members of Dumbledore's Army) was attacked by werewolf Fenrir Greyback and left severely scarred, looking a bit like Alastor Moody's own heavily scarred apperance. 

Now, because Greyback was not transformed and did not bite him, Bill would not become a werewolf, but there would be some changes (in the end, he suddenly developed a liking for very rare steaks.

When the whole family (sans Percy, who was still estranged) and Fleur came to see Bill, Molly despaired at the sight of her eldest son as she applied treatment for her son, lamenting that he was going to get married. Hearing this, Fleur confronted Molly, accusing her (correctly) of believing and perhaps even hoping Fleur would no longer wish to be married to Bill now that he was scarred. Fleur rejected the notion, insisting that Bill's scars only proved his bravery and that she did not care about Bill's looks, believing she was beautiful enough for the both of them before taking over caring for Bill.

Fleur declaring her love for Bill and reaffirming her desire to marry him was the moment where she won the respect of her future in-laws, with Molly offering to give Fleur a tiara from their great-aunt Muriel to use for the wedding (and Fleur agreeing) before the two just hugged each other, taking comfort as they cried over what happened to Bill

On a smaller note, seeing Fleur declare her love for Bill also inspired Tonks to decleare her love for Remus Lupin

Basically the simple analogy is that whatever platform you're using if it has this incrementality testing feature it will create two cohorts or two demographics. So you will have a test group. And what the platform basically does is does a comparison between volume of conversions and conversion rates between the two groups. And that's how it's able to dictate or predict the incremental conversion of a specific campaign or a specific audience or a specific creative. two main reasons why incrementality testing or at least testing it out is worth it and I'll just read these out. - Incrementality Testing: How to Actually Measure Marketing Effectiveness (2026): Kind: captions Language: en Years ago, eBay did something most brands would never consider. [music] They turned off their brand search ads, the ones that show up when you search eBay shoes or eBay electronics. By conventional measurement, these ads looked wildly profitable. So, what happened when eBay turned them off? Well, almost nothing. Traffic and sales stayed flat. The people searching for eBay cameras already wanted to go to eBay. These ads weren't convincing anyone to buy, they were just intercepting the customers eBay already had, and Google was getting paid for it. So, eBay cut the budget on the channel, and that one change saved them millions of dollars per year. Now, [music] here's the uncomfortable question. What would happen if you ran the same test on your best performing channel? Would revenue fall off a cliff because it's truly performing? Or would it stay flat? Most marketers don't actually know the answer, and [music] that's a problem because if you can't answer that question, you might be lighting money on fire and calling it a win. Here's something every marketer has experienced. You're reviewing last quarter's performance, and you pull up your dashboards. Meta says it drove $200,000 in revenue, Google says $400,000, TikTok says $100,000. You add those up, and you get $700,000. That's great. The only problem is that your business only made $450,000 total. The math doesn't work. This isn't a bug, it's just how in-platform attribution works. Ad platforms use what's called deterministic attribution. When someone converts, buys your product, subscribes, downloads your app, whatever, the platform looks backward and asked, "Did this person see or click on one of our ads prior to purchase?" If yes, they count it as a win. But, converted after seeing an ad is not the same thing as converted because of an ad. Even more sophisticated models, like multi-touch attribution, which spread credit across multiple ads instead of giving it all [music] to the last click, still have this same blind spot. They're tracking who saw what, not what actually caused the sale. Some of those people were going to buy anyway. Maybe they heard about you from a friend. Maybe they typed your URL directly into the browser, [music] and your retargeting ad happened to hit them an hour before they checked out. Some of those people were likely driven by multiple different ads, and each ad platform wants to take credit for the whole conversion. In-platform attribution counts all of that as a win for paid ads, but is it? Let's put numbers to this. You spend $10,000 on Meta retargeting ads. The platform reports that people who saw those ads bought $25,000 worth of your product. At a 60% margin, that's $15,000 in gross profit on $10,000 in spend, $5,000 of pure profit. Looks like a no-brainer, we'll do that all day. But, what if half of those people would have bought anyway without ever seeing the Meta retargeting ad? Now, your incremental revenue is $12,500. At a 60% margin, that's 7,500 in gross profit on a $10,000 investment. The platform showed you a winner, but in reality, that campaign just lost you $2,500. This is obviously hypothetical, but it happens constantly. >> [music] >> Ad platforms are incentivized to take credit for as many conversions as possible, and I don't blame them. But, that doesn't mean that those ad platforms [music] actually caused those conversions. This often gets worse over time. When your brand is small and nobody knows who you are, attribution [music] and incrementality are roughly the same thing. You turn on ads, sales spike. It's pretty clear that the ads really are working. But, as the brand scales, everything gets noisier. People hear about your product from friends, you get press coverage, you're running ads on five different channels, word of mouth really starts to kick in. Now, it's no longer obvious what's actually driving purchases, and your attribution dashboards, which looked clean and confident [music] when you were small, start to mislead you. You pour money into channels that look efficient, but aren't really working, while starving the channels that are actually driving growth, but don't get the attribution credit. So, how do you figure out what's real? The answer is incrementality, and it answers a completely different question. Attribution asks, "Did this person convert after seeing my ad?" Incrementality [music] asks, "Would this person have converted anyway, even if they never saw my ad?" That second question is what actually matters because the answer tells you whether your marketing caused the sale or just showed up on the path to conversion. Imagine two parallel universes. In universe A, you ran an ad and the customer bought. In universe B, you didn't run the ad at all. In universe B, did the customer still buy? If they made a purchase in both universes, it means that your ad didn't cause anything, it just happened to be there. If they only bought in universe A, that means that your ad actually drove that incremental impact. The obvious problem is that you can't actually observe both universes at the same time. This is called the counterfactual problem, and it's the fundamental challenge of marketing measurement. Well, how do you solve it? The same way the FDA [music] does. When the FDA, the Food and Drug Administration in the US, tests whether a new drug works or not, they don't just give it to sick people and see who gets better. Some people get better on their own, so that wouldn't prove the drug actually did anything. Instead, they run a controlled experiment. One group gets the drug, another group gets a placebo, same conditions, same time period. The difference in outcomes between those two groups tells us the drug's true causal effect. So, it's a measure of causation, not just correlation. Marketing measurement should work exactly the same [music] way. You need a test group that sees your ads and a control group that doesn't. The difference in outcomes between those groups is your incremental lift, [music] the thing your marketing actually caused. There are a few ways to run these experiments in practice, and they're not all equal. Some ad platforms offer built-in tests. Meta calls theirs conversion lift, and Google has similar tools. [music] These are true randomized control trials. The platform randomly holds back ads from a subset of users and measures the difference. When done correctly, these experiments are scientifically extremely rigorous, but there's obviously a catch. You're trusting the platform to grade its own homework. On the other end of the spectrum, you have go-dark tests. These are very simple. You just turn a channel completely off and see what happens. There doesn't need to be a lot of fancy statistics, just a before and after comparison, but now you're comparing different time periods, not different audiences at the same time. So, seasonality, promotions, and a hundred other variables can contaminate [music] your results. The option in the middle, and the one we think is practical [music] for most brands, is geographic experimentation. Instead of randomizing individual users, you randomize by geography. You increase spend in some regions, you hold other regions constant as your control, and then you compare the outcomes. Your controlled regions tell you what would have happened in your test regions if you hadn't changed anything. That's your counterfactual. That's your universe B. Geographic tests work across most channels. They don't require platform cooperation, and you can run them yourself. The challenge is that your regions won't be perfectly identical. Austin, Texas and Denver, Colorado don't have the same population, the same baseline sales, or the same seasonality patterns. [music] You can't just compare raw numbers between them. The traditional approach to doing this type of measurement in marketing is called matched market testing. The idea is straightforward, you find two cities or two regions that look similar, similar population, similar income levels, similar baseline sales, and you use one as your test market and one as your control. If Austin and Portland have similar demographics and buying patterns, you increase spend [music] in Austin, hold Portland steady, and then compare. But, we can create a blend of cities that allow us to create a synthetic New Orleans that is a better [music] match for New Orleans than any other natural city might be. We could imagine that blend could be a combination of Houston, Texas and Charleston, South Carolina and down in Savannah, Georgia, where the blend is a better match than any of those cities individually could be. [music] So, you decide to test it. Here's exactly what that looks like. First, you need historical data, revenue by geography and by day, at least 90 days, ideally a full year. If you can pull report from Shopify or Google Analytics 4 [music] that shows daily revenue by state or DMA, you have what you need. Then, you upload that data into an experimentation tool, in this case, GeoLift by Recast. [music] The tool charts your data by geography so you can do a quick sanity check. Are there any obvious anomalies, missing data? If it looks [music] clean, you move on. Now, you design the experiment. You tell the tool a few things, that you're planning to increase spend, that you're measuring revenue, roughly what you think the channel ROI might be, that's incremental ROI, very important, how long you want to run the test, and how much budget you're willing to put behind it. The tool then runs simulations across your geographies. It's looking for regions where historically, when one goes up, the other tends to go up, too, meaning that they're good candidates for comparison. It spits out the candidate test configurations ranked by statistical quality. You can click between rows to see how well the synthetic control matches each set of test markets. They test new audiences and new creatives at the same time, which makes it impossible to understand what actually caused the performance change. Instead, the correct approach is to test interests using proven ads only. In other words, the creative is already validated, and it has already shown to work. So, now the audience becomes the variable. For example, if you sell fitness apparel, you might test audiences like CrossFit, Gymshark, or Nike Training Club. Each interest is placed in its own ad set, but all of them use the exact same proven winning ads. This allows you to clearly see whether the audience itself improves performance. Sometimes an interest group reveals a pocket of buyers the algorithm was not prioritizing before. And occasionally, those insights feed back into your broad targeting performance as Meta learns more about the ideal customer profile. Interest testing is not the core driver of performance anymore, but it remains a valuable way to expand reach strategically. Once new prospects enter your ecosystem, the next step is converting those who showed interest but didn't buy. So, step four, set up your retargeting campaign. Not everyone buys the first time they see your product. In fact, most people don't. On average, it takes seven interactions with a brand before a customer will make a purchase. That's why every account needs a dedicated retargeting campaign. This campaign focuses exclusively on people who have already interacted with your brand. So, typical retargeting audiences include website visitors from the last 30 days, people who added products to their cart, and social media engagers. These audiences already know who you are, which means your messaging should look a little different from the first two campaigns. Instead of introducing the brand, retargeting ads should focus on reminding people about products they viewed, showing social proof, addressing objections, and highlighting urgency or offers. The important rule here is that this campaign should only target these audiences. Meta sometimes tries to expand beyond retargeting audiences, which can cause spend to leak back into prospecting. So, to avoid this, make sure audience expansion settings are turned off, so the campaign stays tightly focused. Retargeting campaigns typically run with smaller budgets than prospecting campaigns, but they often produce some of the highest conversion rates in your account, because this is your warmer audience. Once someone finally makes a purchase, the next opportunity begins. So, step five, drive repeat purchases with a retention campaign. Many advertisers make the mistake of treating a customer's first purchase as the end of the buying journey, but in reality, it's just the beginning. Your retention campaign exists to turn customers into repeat buyers. This campaign targets only people who have already purchased from your brand before. However, not all customers are the same. Someone who bought last week behaves very differently from someone who bought a year ago. That's why retention should usually be split into two audiences. First is recent buyers, typically customers from the last 180 days. These people already remember your brand, so your ads can focus on complimentary products, upsells, or new releases. And then the second one, older buyers, customers who purchased further in the past. These audiences may need reminders on your brand overall, seasonal offers, or product updates to bring them back. Retention campaigns are extremely powerful because the cost of acquiring a repeat customer is usually much lower than acquiring a brand new one. When done correctly, they increase customer lifetime value and improve the overall profitability of your ad account. The reason this campaign structure works so well overall is that it separates different marketing objectives into their own environments. Your prospecting campaign focuses entirely on finding new customers. Your scaling campaign pushes winning ads harder. Interest testing allows you to explore new audiences without confusing the algorithm. Retargeting converts people who have already showed interest, and retention campaigns generate repeat purchases from existing customers. So, instead of one messy account where everything overlaps, you now have a system where each campaign has a clear purpose. And that clarity makes optimization easier, protects your best ads, maximizes your dollar, and gives Meta's algorithm cleaner signals to work with. If you implement this structure correctly, your ad account will get far easier to scale because every part of the system is designed to do one job extremely well. And if you want more breakdowns of real strategies that are working right now in Facebook and Instagram ads, make sure to subscribe because the platforms evolve constantly and the small business owners who adapt to their ad systems the fastest are always the ones who continue to profit.

- What is AI Data Management? Discover, Clean, & Secure Data with AI: Kind: captions Language: en What is AI data management? Well, consider the data management life cycle. So we have a collection stage, a data collection stage. We have a data cleaning stage, a data analysis stage, and then a data governance stage. And this is all in a life cycle, well, AI data management is simply using AI technologies to help automate or streamline each of these stages, and the goal is to make enterprise data accurate, accessible and secure so organizations can fully use it, which is easier said than done because we're usually talking about a lot of data here. Now in a recent information management report, 64% of organizations said that they manage at least one petabyte of data, and that data is rarely in one place. It's spread out across many systems and formats. So let's take a look at four ways that AI data management can help, starting with data discovery. So businesses receive data from all sorts of places. That could be internal databases, it is, it could be. From cloud services, it could be IOT sensors, just to name a few. And this data often ends up distributed in silos in different places, so across different departments or different cloud accounts or different local machines, and often with no central visibility. Now, there's a term for this and it's called shadow data, and shadow data means data assets that an organization isn't managing might not even be aware of. And if you can't see your data, you don't know where it is, or even if it exists at all, there's not much you can do with it. In fact, it's estimated that 68% of an organization's data goes unanalyzed and therefore unused. So that's two thirds of data that may be dark data stored at cost, but providing no value. So how can AI data management help us out? Well essentially, AI can automate data discovery. So let's think about how it can do that. One way is using something called smart classification. Now machine learning algorithms can learn to classify data by content. So for example, by analyzing the contents of a file, we can determine if a document is a contract or an invoice or a resume. By automatically labeling the data with metadata, these tools make hidden data more visible and more searchable. Now, NLP, or Natural Language Processing, plays a part in smart classification, but it can also be used for processing unstructured text. For example, an NLP system could parse thousands of free-form text documents like emails and reports. It can pull out entities from those documents, like names, dates, or product codes, and therefore effectively turn that unstructured text. Into structured records in a catalog. And AI can also help with relationships as well. Specifically, relationships detection. Now, this is inferring relationships between different data sets, like how maybe item SKU in an e-commerce database corresponds to a product ID in a warehouse spreadsheet. All of this helps in discovering data linkages across silos. So that's data discovery, but what about data quality? Well, it's all very well getting access to data. That's great, we need this data. But what if this data is actually bad data? Bad data can cause more problems than no data at all. Because if data is inaccurate or it's inconsistent or incomplete or just outdated, the AI models or business decisions based on it will be unreliable. So how can AI data management help us out here? Well, some of the low hanging fruit comes just with some basic automated data cleansing operations. Now this is basic stuff like validating that all entries in a column follow a valid format and fixing those that don't, but AI-powered data management can also help fill in fields with missing values entirely. And that is using something called synthetic data generation. Now, what this is doing is it's supplying plausible values where no values were otherwise provided. So if a salary value is missing, the AI system could predict that value based on somebody's role, and their experience, and their location, by learning from other complete records. Now there's a careful path to trade here because a good estimate can be better than having no value, but straight up bad data from a poor forecast causes, as we've said, more problems than no data at all. Now the pattern matching capabilities of AI make it very well suited anomaly detection. This is detecting anomalies in specific data sets. AI algorithms can profile a data set and alert when incoming data doesn't fit past patterns. So if a daily sales file usually has about 100,000 rows and then suddenly it has a million rows, well, an AI observability tool will flag that as a potential data issue. These AI techniques reduce the need for humans to painstakingly clean the data and they work hand-in-hand with rules-based approaches based on business rules, like a order value cannot be a negative value. So that's data quality. Now even if data is collected and cleaned it's only valuable if people can get to it when needed. Data accessibility issues arise when data is locked in silos or when the data is only available via a complex tool or some sort of restricted cumbersome process. Data silos and slow access, they do more than just frustrate users, they can also lead to inconsistent versions of the truth, because different teams rely on whatever subset of data they can just get a hold of. So there's things we can do for this, and one thing we can is we can streamline data integration, which is the process of combining data from different sources. So this is one way that AI data management can help because traditionally data engineers had to write ETL pipelines with lots of manual mapping rules, but now AI enabled integration tools can automatically detect relationships between data sets and then suggest how to join or merge them together. Now, natural language data query is a method that lets people query and interact with data just by asking. So instead of writing code or SQL queries, user can ask show me last quarter's sales by region in plain English and then an AI powered system will understand the intent, translate that into an appropriate database query and then return the result. And then also we have adaptive controls as well. So adaptive access controls determines who can access the information. So rather than applying a static rule that either allows or denies access to a whole data source, AI-driven systems can implement contextual access, detecting what a user typically accesses and then applying those same access rules to other datasets where permissions have not yet been manually granted. And that brings us nicely on to the final topic. You see, I've got this nagging voice in my head telling me that no discussion about AI data management is complete. Without discussing data security. Hey, Martin, what about data security? Yeah, that voice. Well, the problem statement for data security today is basically, how do we enforce all of the policies and detect threats when there's so much new data coming along? And this is where AI is increasingly being applied. Now, traditionally, data loss protection, Well, that was really relying on rules. So for example, a rule to detect credit card numbers and to block them from being emailed, but AI driven DLP tools, they can detect much more than just things that look like a credit card sequence. An AI model can detect all sorts of personally identifiable information or learn what a source code file looks like versus a financial document. Once that data has been classified correctly, rules-based policies can then make sure it's protected. Now, another one is UEBA. That's user and entity behavior analytics, and that can employ Ai to monitor how users typically access data and then to flag deviations. And then one we're probably all familiar with is fraud detection. Those are algorithms that can analyze transaction data in real time to spot fraudulent patterns that a set of predefined rules just might not catch. In essence, AI complements the traditional rules-based security measures by adding a layer of smart surveillance and adaptive control. Ultimately, when data is discoverable and clean and accessible, it fuels more informed insights and better decision making. AI data management can help make that a reality by bringing greater control and consistency to how data is used.
