- ¿Por qué tus antepasados dormían mejor que tú?: Kind: captions Language: en Welcome, curious minds. Do you know how our ancestors slept thousands of years ago? How many hours of sleep do we really need each day depending on our age? And what happens to our bodies and brains if we don't get enough sleep? Is it really dangerous to wake a sleepwalker? Has it ever happened to you that just as you're falling asleep, you suddenly feel like you're falling into a void and you jump out of bed? Why does that happen? Have you ever stopped to think about how strange the act of sleeping is? Every night we lie down, close our eyes, and our brain completely disconnects from the outside world. At that moment, our bodies are paralyzed, our senses shut down , and we are at the mercy of any danger. From an evolutionary point of view, the loss of consciousness during sleep is one of the riskiest acts in the entire animal kingdom. We spend a third of our lives—think about it, an average of 25 years—sleeping, and therefore defenseless against environmental threats. And yet, this state is a fundamental pillar for our survival. We need sleep because it is the essential biological mechanism by which our body and brain repair themselves, rebalance, and prepare to face a new day. During rest, we not only conserve energy but also carry out crucial maintenance functions. The immune system strengthens its defenses to fight infections. Muscle tissue regenerates, and at a neurological level, the brain processes emotions, consolidates memory, and uses the lymphatic system to cleanse toxins accumulated from intense neuronal activity during the day. In short, sleep is not a luxury or a state of inactivity, but an active and vital process without which our physical health, mental stability, and cognitive abilities would quickly collapse. But how did our bodies come to design such a complex yet vulnerable sleep system ? It didn't arise by chance, but was forged by evolution under extreme conditions. To understand how modern Homo sapiens sleep, we have to travel back to the African savanna millions of years ago, to the dawn of humanity. Imagine for a moment a hostile environment, a pitch-black night where the only sound is that of nocturnal predators stalking in the darkness. In that era, the first hominins, the evolutionary branch unique to humans among hominids, had no houses, no doors, no walls. To avoid attacks from big cats, our ancestors had to resort to a strategy still used today by our evolutionary cousins, such as chimpanzees and orangutans: building nests in the highest branches of trees. Sleeping high up prevented you from becoming a cheetah's dinner, but the price to pay was very high, to say the least. Imagine the stress of trying to rest knowing that one wrong move could send you plummeting to the ground. For this reason, the sleep of our ancestors in the trees was light and fragmented. They woke up constantly. To avoid falling, their muscles had to maintain a constant state of tension, and this tension prevented their bodies from truly relaxing, making it nearly impossible to regularly reach the deepest stages of sleep. Today's non-human hominins—chimpanzees, bonobos, gorillas, and orangutans—still suffer from this limitation. Their sleep is a kind of half-wakefulness. But then something happened that changed the fate of our species forever. We managed to domesticate fire when species like Homo erectus learned to control the flames. They not only gained light and heat to warm themselves, but also a protective shield. Fire acted as a security wall, a perimeter of light that kept wild animals away. For the first time in evolutionary history, these hominins could abandon the protection of branches and sleep on solid ground. This change was revolutionary for a biological reason you might not imagine. Lying on the ground next to a fire, the need to remain alert to avoid falling from a tree disappeared completely. His muscles were finally able to relax, and this complete loss of muscle tone is an essential requirement for the brain to fully enter REM sleep. At this point, we should explain that each night our rest is divided into two main states. Non-REM sleep. Non-REM sleep occupies 75% of our night and is divided into three stages of increasing depth, from the lightest, stages one and two, to stage three, which is when the body releases growth hormone to repair tissues and strengthen the immune system. It is also when the lymphatic system, which we mentioned earlier, is activated, and it is responsible for eliminating toxins accumulated during the day. Scientifically, it is the most valuable period for physical health. If you don't reach enough stage three, your immune system doesn't update properly, and tissues don't repair correctly, accelerating biological aging. And then there is REM sleep. After deep sleep, the brain shifts gears and enters REM sleep, which stands for rapid eye movement. Here, brain activity surges to levels almost identical to those of wakefulness, but the body undergoes total muscle paralysis to prevent us from acting out in real life what we are experiencing in the dream. REM sleep is the time when the brain sorts through memories, discards the unnecessary, and consolidates learning. It is also the setting for our most vivid and narrative dreams. If deep sleep repairs the body, REM sleep repairs the mind and regulates our emotions. Without it, we become irritable and lose the ability to concentrate. British neuroscientist Matthew Walker, author of the essay *Why We Sleep*, argues that the transition hominins made to longer, deeper REM sleep was the catalyst that triggered our cognitive abilities. By sleeping on the ground, protected by fire, and experiencing deeper sleep, the brains of our ancestors could process the day's emotions, soothe traumatic memories, and consolidate what they had learned. Upon awakening, those early humans possessed more creative minds, capable of innovating, crafting more complex tools, and developing something as sophisticated as articulate language. Fire not only warmed our bodies, it triggered a neurochemical revolution that allowed us to sleep deeply and evolve into what we are today. Did you know that we are the primate that sleeps the least, yet sleeps the most deeply? Modern great apes spend more hours sleeping. For example, chimpanzees, bonobos, and gorillas spend an average of 10 hours in their nests, and orangutans, the sleepiest of all, almost 13. However, their rest is light and fragmented because, as we've explained, they can't afford to completely shut down their brains in the trees. In contrast, when our ancestors descended to Earth, evolution compressed their rest, as remaining on the ground was risky. Despite fire, they became efficient sleepers, sleeping fewer hours, an average of seven or eight. But in return, the time they spent in that restorative REM phase skyrocketed to reach 20 or 25% of their total sleep, an absolute record compared to any other primate. The chimpanzee, with whom we share more than 98% of our DNA, is the only one that comes close. So, when did we diverge from the rest of the primates in terms of sleep? When exactly did the miracle occur that allowed hominins to begin domesticating fire? Experts disagree . Some researchers believe it must have happened 1.5 million years ago, while others are more cautious and explain that solid evidence that our ancestors could consistently use fire is no more than 500,000 years old. Has it ever happened to you that just as you're falling asleep, you suddenly feel like you're falling and you jump up in bed? This phenomenon is known as a hypnic jerk. And evolutionary biologists believe this muscle spasm is a direct echo of our arboreal past. If your body relaxes Very quickly upon falling asleep, our primal brain panics, interpreting it as a real fall from a branch and sending an emergency electrical shock to our muscles to make us grab onto an imaginary tree trunk. Perhaps our body is resting on a comfortable mattress, but our brain is still on the African savanna. And speaking of survival, why do we tend to sleep so poorly the first night we spend in a hotel room or someone else's house? Sleep science has discovered that it's a pure and simple defense mechanism known as the first-night effect. Just as ducks or dolphins can sleep with half their brain awake to monitor their surroundings, humans employ a slightly more subtle version. During that first night in unfamiliar territory, one of our brain hemispheres, usually the left, refuses to enter the deep sleep phase. It remains in a state of light alertness, acting as a night watchman in case any threats appear in this new environment. In a recent 2026 study, research from Japan's Nagoya University pinpointed the exact chemical switch that triggers this sleeplessness. They discovered that upon entering a new place, specific neurons in our amygdala, the brain region that controls our most primal emotions, are activated and release a molecule called neurotensin. This travels to the substantia nigra, the area of the brain that controls wakefulness, and gives it the strict order to maintain a state of alertness. In other words, that first night in a hotel, you don't sleep badly because of the mattress. It's your own biology flooding your brain with neurotensin to protect you from invisible predators. And the best part of this discovery is that by unraveling this circuit, scientists are already envisioning the development of new treatments for insomnia that can switch off this excessive state of alertness. The search for comfort by the Homo genus didn't stop at bare ground. If we look for the archaeological origin of beds, we have to travel to the Border Cave site in South Africa. According to a 2020 article published in the journal Science, a team of archaeologists led by South African Lin Watley discovered what we can consider humanity's first mattress. It is approximately 200,000 years old. These early humans gathered broad-leaved grasses, especially from the Panicaceae subfamily, such as Guinea grass, which still grows at the cave entrance. But what is most striking is that they didn't simply throw these grasses onto the ground; they placed them on thick layers of ash. The ash acted as a natural insect repellent, providing them with a soft, warm, and bite-free surface. Furthermore, among the remains in Border Cave, sprigs of camphor tree were found— an aromatic plant of the Tarconanthus species that is still used today in rural areas of East Africa to repel mosquitoes. So they knew exactly what they were doing. By creating pest-free spaces, these humans improved their health, avoided parasitic diseases , and achieved higher-quality sleep, crucial for cognitive development. As more complex civilizations emerged, the concept of rest evolved into forms that would seem, well, incomprehensible to us today. Let's talk, for example, about pillows. What's the first thing you look for when you rest your head on one? Softness, right? Well, if we travel to ancient Egypt, we'll discover that the upper classes didn't use soft pillows, but rather rigid headrests carved from stone, wood, ivory, or alabaster. Imagine trying to sleep with your skull resting just above your ear on a hard structure with a flat base, a central column, and a concave top support. It sounds like a torture device, but it actually had very practical uses. First, in a hot desert, elevating the head allowed air currents to circulate around the neck, offering thermal relief impossible to achieve with fabric cushions. Aesthetically, These headrests protected the elaborate hairstyles and expensive wigs of the Egyptian elite. And on a survival level, keeping the nose and ears off the ground prevented scorpions or spiders from entering during the night, but their usefulness went even further. For the Egyptians, sleep also meant entering a dangerous spiritual world. That's why these headrests possessed a profound religious and magical significance. They were often decorated with representations of protective deities like Bes and Taweret, responsible for warding off evil spirits that lurked in the darkness and tried to enter through the skull's openings at night. One of the most emblematic examples of these pillows belonged to Pharaoh Tutankhamun and was discovered along with the rest of the Egyptian king's tomb by British archaeologist Howard Carter. This headrest was made of elephant ivory and carved with the figure of Su, the god of air and light, who raised the pharaoh's head to ensure his daily rebirth. Since the head was considered the seat of the spirit, this object was so vital that it was included in tombs as an indispensable amulet from the Book of the Dead to ensure resurrection in the afterlife. And how did the indigenous cultures of the Americas rest? In these lands, long before the arrival of Europeans, the natives developed sleeping technologies that were not only masterpieces of climate adaptation but also possessed symbolic and spiritual significance. To understand this, we must discuss two inventions that are thousands of years old: the petate and the hammock. In Mesoamerica, the king of sleeping mats was the petate, a type of mat or rug woven from palm, cane, or guano fibers. But for civilizations like the Mexica, Maya, and Chontal, the petate was much more than a simple mattress on the ground. It was the symbol of the human cycle, the artifact that linked birth and death. In fact, in pre-Hispanic Mexico, midwives used it to receive newborns; that is, life began on its interwoven fibers. Throughout their lives, a person ate, prayed, loved, and slept on it. And when death came, the petate became their shroud, serving as a coffin to bury the body. You were born on a petate and you left this world wrapped in it. It was a highly respected object. If we move south to the tropical zones, the Caribbean coasts, the jungles of South America, the petate ceased to be practical due to the stifling heat and extreme humidity. It was in these areas that one of history's greatest innovations, over 4,000 years old, was born: the hammock. In some cultures, the hammock is known as the cradle of the gods. The creation of hammocks was a highly specialized female task that required advanced knowledge of cotton weaving, the agibisco. From an evolutionary and comfort standpoint, sleeping suspended in the air in a tropical environment was a very clever adaptation because it offered unparalleled ventilation to combat the extreme heat and, more importantly, kept the individual away from the dampness of the ground and dangerous fauna such as insects, snakes, and other crawling animals. When Europeans arrived in America, they greatly appreciated these inventions. In fact, later, in the tropical and coastal areas of the viceroyalties of New Spain and Peru, the population continued to use native tools such as the hammock and the pedate (a type of hammock), while in the colder mountainous areas, attempts were made to replicate European customs of thermal insulation. Europeans, especially sailors, immediately adopted the hammock upon realizing that sleeping suspended prevented them from falling out of bed due to the rocking of ships. This forever changed the history of navigation. But before continuing, let's go back in time a bit to the Middle Ages in Europe to tell you some surprising facts. Because you think that sleeping stretched out horizontally, as we do now, has always been the norm? Well, no. In the Middle Ages and well into the modern era, a large part of the population slept in a semi-seated position. They lay propped up on numerous cushions to elevate their torsos. This wasn't an extravagant fashion, but rather a belief based on humoral theory and contemporary medical texts, which held that sleeping completely flat hindered digestion. It was thought that the lack of inclination allowed malignant vapors, or humors, from the stomach to rise to the brain and cause illness, including serious mental disorders . Adding to this physiological reason was a psychological fear. Sleeping horizontally was associated with death because lying on one's back was the position in which corpses were placed in their coffins and graves. The fear of suffering a sudden death during the night prompted people to sleep almost upright, ready to react or at least to establish a very clear visual distinction between sleep and death. European furniture of the time also reflected the harshness of living conditions. In northern regions like Brittany, Scotland, and the Netherlands, box beds became popular. These were sturdy wooden pieces of furniture, similar to large wardrobes, equipped with hinged doors or thick curtains, into which people would go to sleep. And although they might seem like a luxury item, these box beds were also a lifesaver for peasants in the colder regions of Europe. For a humble family sharing a single stone room with their farm animals, this rustic piece of furniture was their only protection against the night's chill and rats. Closing the bed doors also created a microclimate that retained body heat. These box beds sometimes had interior shelves for storing valuables and served as protective shelters for young children against wolves or stray livestock on the farms. However, forget the privacy and intimacy we have today, because people didn't sleep alone in their beds. It was still a shared social space. Parents, children, sometimes visitors, and even some pets, which provided additional warmth, could all sleep on the same mattress. In the case of wealthier people, even the closest and most trusted servants would occasionally share the bed with their masters, ready to be at their beck and call. This not only kept them warm but also provided a greater sense of security. You have to imagine the nighttime atmosphere in medieval cities, saturated with foul odors due to the lack of sanitation. This reinforced the fear of miasmas, considered malignant effluvia or corrupt air emanating from decomposing organic matter, stagnant water, and diseased bodies. At that time, it was believed that these nauseating smells traveling through the air transmitted contagious diseases like cholera or the plague. Therefore, isolating oneself in closed beds or sleeping surrounded by people was perceived as a shield, a vital barrier against the diseases that lurked in the darkness. However, for most servants, rest was far more precarious. In castles and wealthy homes, it was common for servants, soldiers, and vassals to spend the night on straw mattresses on the floor of the great hall. These rudimentary cloth sacks, filled with straw or cheap wool, were unrolled each night around the central fire. At dawn, these makeshift mattresses were hastily gathered up so the room could resume its usual daytime activity. Overcrowding, smoke, and fleas were the constant companions of this type of communal rest. In reality, it's quite similar to what our Paleolithic ancestors did: sleeping huddled together in groups, always alert to ensure survival against any threat. Did you know that our current obsession with sleeping eight hours straight is a very modern invention? For millennia, and documented from the time of Homer in ancient Greece until the end of the 10th century, human beings did not sleep straight through the night, but rather our sleep was biphasic, that is, we slept in two distinct phases of about 4 hours each, separated by a brief period Staying awake at night was common among medieval Europeans. The most interesting thing is that all of this relates to a question you may have asked yourselves: Why do I sometimes wake up at 3 a.m. and can't fall back asleep? I get anxious thinking I have severe insomnia. Of course, if you suspect insomnia, consult a professional. But it's possible that your body is trying to return to that primal sleep pattern our ancestors had. Or at least that's what can be deduced from an experiment conducted in the early 1990s by psychiatrist and researcher Thomas Ware, a scientist at the National Institute of Mental Health in the United States. Ware subjected a group of volunteers to a natural photoperiod, that is, he eliminated all artificial light and exposed them to 14 hours of darkness per day, simulating the long winter nights of the pre-industrial era. For the first few weeks, the participants slept an average of 11 hours straight, trying to compensate for all the sleep deprivation accumulated from the demands of modern life. However, after a month, their sleep patterns underwent a change that surprised the researchers. Uninterrupted sleep disappeared completely. Instead, it gave way to a segmented or biphasic pattern. The subjects slept for an initial four-hour block, woke for one or two hours, and then fell back asleep for a second four-hour block until dawn. And what was most interesting was what happened during the waking interval between these two phases. The participants didn't experience frustration or stress, nor did they toss and turn in bed. On the contrary, endocrinological tests revealed high levels of prolactin, a hormone associated with calm and relaxation. This induced a meditative and peaceful state of consciousness, ideal for reflection. This biological finding found its counterpart in research conducted by the American historian Roger Eksch. After dedicating years to scrutinizing diaries, court records, and medical literature from past centuries to write his work, At the End of the Night, he concluded that segmented sleep was the universal norm before gas lighting and later electricity entered human life . In pre-industrial societies, people retired to rest shortly after sunset, experienced an initial sleep, and awoke around midnight. This intermediate period of activity, known as the vigil, possessed immense cultural and social richness. In the intimacy of the twilight, people tended the hearth fire, conversed with family and neighbors, prayed, interpreted their recent dreams, or reflected in solitude. Furthermore, medical manuals recommended this time as the most optimal for reproduction, arguing that the body was rested after the initial sleep. We find evidence of this practice in the literature of the Spanish Golden Age. Miguel de Cervantes captured this habit in Don Quixote, where he explicitly mentions how the protagonist completes his first dream, presupposing the existence of a subsequent waking state and a second rest. Likewise, poets and playwrights like López de Vega and Quevedo alluded to the moments of inspiration or spiritual tribulation that arose in the early hours of the morning, when the silence of the surroundings fostered mental acuity. Some experts point out that the suppression of this hour of creative wakefulness through the imposition of artificial light has deprived modern humanity of a valuable space for introspection. And since we're talking about harnessing the creativity of the night, there's a historical anecdote that tells of geniuses like the inventor Thomas Edison and the painter Salvador Dalí, who hated wasting time sleeping, knowing that the hypnagogic phase—those moments of drowsiness before falling completely asleep—is a goldmine for creativity and imagination. So they used a trick to make the most of it. They sat down to rest in a chair with some heavy keys, They would hold metal balls in their hands and place a plate on the floor. The instant they lost consciousness and entered deep sleep, the muscles in their hands would relax, the keys would fall onto the plate, and the noise would jolt them awake. Yes, they managed to capture those brilliant, almost dreamlike ideas before deep sleep erased them from their minds forever. But then, where does the myth that humans need eight hours of uninterrupted sleep to rest properly come from? The blame lies with the Industrial Revolution, which began around 1760. With the rise of manufacturing and the widespread use of gas lighting from the early 19th century, and a few decades later with electricity, the night became an extension of the workday. Workers' time ceased to be governed by solar cycles and was subjected to the tyranny of the clock, becoming the property of industry. Capitalist society demanded that human rest be compressed into a single, efficient block so that people would be ready to produce at dawn. So, if they deviated from this schedule, it was taken as a sign of laziness. We force our biology to adapt to machine schedules, but our biology is stubborn. Have you ever felt judged for not being able to get up early with energy, or conversely, been surprised that you couldn't keep your eyes open past 10 p.m.? Modern society rewards early risers and labels night owls as lazy. But evolutionary anthropology tells us something very different. Canadian biological anthropologist David R. Samson, a researcher at the University of Toronto and author of the book *Award Tribal Future*, formulated a theory known as the sentinel effect. Samson lived with the Hatza, a hunter-gatherer community in Tanzania that lives without electricity, and monitored their activity patterns using biometric devices. Samson discovered that in a group of 30 people, the total amount of time all members were awake at the same time throughout the night barely reached 18 minutes. There was always someone awake, tending the fire or keeping watch. This extreme asynchrony isn't a disruption of circadian rhythms—that is, the internal 24- hour biological clock that regulates sleep-wake cycles, body temperature, hormones, and metabolism in response to light and darkness. The Jazza's asynchrony is a defense mechanism, a genetic strategy designed to ensure collective survival. In wild environments, having individuals with different chronotypes ensures that a percentage of the group is always awake. Larks, those who are naturally early risers, and owls, those who stay alert late, complement each other to detect approaching predators or rival tribes. So, if you're a night owl forced to get up at 6 a.m. for the office, you're not lazy. You are going against your physiology and are victims of a modern world that ignores our evolutionary heritage. This imposition of modern norms on ancestral organisms generates a profound biological shock, leading us to analyze sleep disorders from an anthropological perspective. American researcher Carol Wman, a professor at Emory University, has thoroughly studied what she calls the ecology of sleep in traditional cultures in places like Egypt, Vietnam, and Papua New Guinea. While most of us invest significant resources in seeking absolute silence, ergonomic mattresses, and total isolation for sleep, pre-industrial societies rest in the opposite acoustic context. They sleep in noisy environments surrounded by familiar breathing, domestic animals, crying children, and conversations around the fire. Because for the mind sculpted during the Paleolithic era, the noise of their social group is an unequivocal indicator of safety. It signifies that the tribe is present and alert. Silence, on the other hand, sends an alarm signal to the primitive brain, suggesting that the group has dispersed or that an imminent threat has caused the animals to fall silent. This dissonance This explains why some people experience high levels of anxiety in the complete stillness of their modern bedrooms and require white noise or the hum of a television to fall asleep. The modern environment, devoid of social stimuli, stresses a nervous system calibrated for group life. Adding to the lack of social interaction is the great enemy of our rest: artificial light. At a biological level, our bodies are designed to secrete melatonin, the hormone that regulates the sleep-wake cycle, as sunlight fades and temperatures drop. Despite this, today we live out of sync with the solar cycle. We deceive our retinal photoreceptors with the blue light emitted from the screens of mobile phones, tablets, and televisions right up until the moment we close our eyes. This blue light suppresses melatonin synthesis and induces an unnatural state of hyperactivation. The chronic insomnia suffered by a large part of the world's population is now considered an evolutionary anomaly. We are subjecting Paleolithic organisms to digital light chaos. In fact, comparative studies conducted with members of the Gatza tribes in Tanzania or the Saan of the Kalahari Desert in Namibia show that in these communities it is very rare to find someone complaining of not being able to sleep. Their rest periods, which range between 6 and 7 hours, are synchronized exclusively with the drop in temperatures after sunset and the physical exertion accumulated during the day, demonstrating that the lack of rest is largely a product of our contemporary lifestyle. Current science, supported by institutions such as the National Sleep Foundation, tells us that there is no universal magic number regarding the hours we need to sleep, but rather that it all depends on our age. In general, a newborn needs between 14 and 17 hours a day for their nervous system to develop. A preschool child, aged 3 to 5, needs between 10 and 13 hours of sleep, while during the school years, between 6 and 13, the brain requires between 9 and 11 hours to consolidate everything it learns. During adolescence, the body still demands between 8 and 10 hours, which explains why teenagers find it so hard to get up early. It is in adulthood, between 18 and 64 years of age, that the biological need stabilizes within a range of 7 to 9 hours, and as we age, from 65 onwards, our brain usually finds 8 to 10 hours sufficient. After hearing these figures, some of you might be thinking, "My baby doesn't even come close to sleeping 14 or 17 hours; they sleep much less, and only about three hours at a time." But from an anthropological point of view, the expectation that a newborn will sleep many hours at a stretch makes no biological sense. Unlike other mammals such as foals or calves that are born ready to walk, humans are born in a state of extreme immaturity. Our babies are fetuses outside the womb. Their stomachs are tiny and they need constant nourishment. Moreover, their circadian rhythm takes months to develop. At first, they don't even distinguish between day and night. In hunter-gatherer tribes, babies slept in constant physical contact with their mother or other caregivers and woke often for brief feedings before returning to sleep feeling protected. Today, we have placed those same Paleolithic babies in solitary cribs, in separate rooms, and in absolute silence, and we become frustrated when they wake up crying. That nighttime crying is not a fault of the baby, nor is it trying to manipulate us. It is its survival instinct. Its biology tells it that if left alone in the dark, a predator might attack. Despite this, sleep training methods that encourage parents to let their babies cry until they are exhausted in order to accustom them to sleeping longer stretches have become popular in recent decades. However, experts in neuroscience and developmental psychology have criticized this practice, considering it a serious mistake. When a baby cries without being comforted, their brain enters a state of panic. And it triggers a spike in cortisol levels, the stress hormone. Medical studies have shown that after several days of applying these methods, children stop crying and fall asleep. Some might say, "Test passed, but at what cost? Their stress levels remain sky-high." In other words, they appear calm on the outside, but inside their nervous system is still on high alert. They haven't learned to manage their emotions. They've suffered from learned helplessness. Their brains have reached the terrible conclusion that asking for help is useless because no one is going to come to their rescue, which in the long run can affect their emotional regulation and the bond of attachment with their parents. The problem isn't babies' sleep, but the artificial and harmful expectations that modern society imposes on families. And since we're talking about protecting children's sleep, it's important to make a point for those of you who have recently become parents. To prevent the dreaded Sudden Infant Death Syndrome (SIDS), the sudden and medically unexplained death of a baby, infants should always sleep on their backs on a firm surface, without pillows or stuffed animals nearby. Studies show that these guidelines reduce the likelihood of SIDS, as they prevent overheating and ensure that the airways remain clear. This is crucial in a species whose babies are born, as we have mentioned, with extreme neurological immaturity . Furthermore, pediatric consensus states that for at least the first six months of life, the safest place for them is their own crib, located in the parents' room. This avoids the dangers of suffocation in an adult bed, while allowing the newborn's primitive brain to calm down by feeling the close breathing and presence of their caregivers. Likewise, feeling the parents' breathing not only soothes the baby but also acts as a kind of biological pacemaker. The sound and breathing rhythm of an adult help the newborn's immature nervous system synchronize its own inhalation and exhalation rhythms, which are still unstable during those first six months. And since we're talking about difficult nights, before addressing other issues, we should pause to consider a universal experience we've all suffered since childhood: nightmares. Why does our brain, instead of letting us rest peacefully after a tiring day, torture us with images of chases, falls, or monsters? For a long time, science considered that bad dreams were caused by stress, a system failure, or indigestion . But Finnish researcher and cognitive psychologist Antibonsuo revolutionized this idea by proposing that nightmares serve a crucial evolutionary survival purpose . He dubbed this the threat simulation theory. According to Rebonsuo, nightmares act as a kind of virtual reality simulator that we've had since the dawn of humanity. In that period, reacting quickly to a lion attack or the threat of a rival tribe meant the difference between life and death. To ensure our survival, the brain took advantage of REM sleep, the time when we dream vividly and our muscles are paralyzed, to recreate high-risk scenarios in the safe environment of our beds. Through nightmares, the human brain forced us to rehearse escapes, detect threats, and practice defensive motor responses. This way, if a real danger crossed our path the next day, our neural networks had already trained us to flee. Today, it's rare that we have to flee a predator on the savanna, but our brain still uses this old nocturnal simulator to process our modern anxieties, forcing us to deal with stress to prepare us for real-world problems. Understanding that nightmares are essentially a survival rehearsal helps us see them differently. We know they occur mainly during REM sleep, which is when we normally... We wake up. So when we open our eyes, it's easier to remember the fear and the threat. But what happens when the brain short-circuits? The fear leaves the world of dreams, and the person seems awake and terrified, but in reality, they remember nothing the next day. This is where we enter a phenomenon that often worries parents: night terrors. We often lump them together with nightmares, but neurologically, they are very different scenarios. Nightmares, as we've said, usually occur during REM sleep, the stage in which we have the most vivid dreams. If a child or an adult has a nightmare, they wake up scared, recognize you instantly, and the next morning are able to remember the monster that was chasing them. Night terrors, on the other hand, are a system failure in our brain. They occur during slow-wave sleep, the deepest phase, which usually happens in the first third of the night. What happens is that there is a partial awakening. The motor and autonomic nervous systems are suddenly activated, triggering the primitive fight-or-flight response. The person may sit up in bed, scream, sweat, and have their eyes wide open. They appear to be in a state of panic, but therein lies the great mystery. Their conscious brain remains asleep. The one screaming is not the rational child, but their amygdala. That's why, during a night terror, the child doesn't recognize you , and trying to reason with them is useless. In fact, if you try to hug them, they will likely struggle even more. And, most astonishingly, the next morning they won't remember a thing. What causes these episodes? Science indicates that they result from an immaturity of the central nervous system in transitioning between the different stages of sleep. This is why they are so common in childhood and tend to disappear in adolescence. They are often caused by accumulated sleep deprivation, fever, or spikes in stress, although they seem like something out of a horror movie and are distressing for anyone who witnesses them. Clinically, they are generally harmless. The medical recommendation is clear: never try to wake the person by force. Simply ensure the environment is safe so they don't bump into anything, remain calm, and wait a few minutes for the brain to reconnect and return to deep sleep. Not only children can experience them, but also teenagers and adults. In these cases, the main triggers are severe sleep deprivation , sustained stress, a strong hereditary genetic component, alcohol consumption that disrupts the sleep-wake cycle, or even respiratory disorders that fragment the night, such as sleep apnea. When the brain reaches bed exhausted or stressed, the biological pressure of falling into deep sleep is so great that any stimulus triggers that incomplete and uncontrolled awakening. After discussing nightmares and night terrors, another mystery arises, one that occurs right on the border between wakefulness and rest. Surely you have asked yourself this question at some point, or know someone who has. that she asked herself in anguish. What are those shadows I see in the room when I fall asleep? Science calls this phenomenon hypnagogic hallucinations if they occur while falling asleep or hypnopompic hallucinations if they happen upon waking. Often, this state is accompanied by an even more terrifying experience: sleep paralysis. During this transition period, our brain suffers a synchronization mismatch. The muscle paralysis typical of REM sleep, designed by evolution to prevent us from acting out our dreams and injuring ourselves , is activated or persists while our conscious brain is already awake. The result is that the person has their eyes open, but cannot move a single muscle , and their brain begins to mix dream images with the perception of the real world. Clinical studies have documented that during these episodes we usually experience two main types of hallucinations. The first is the intrusive type, The first type involves feeling a malevolent presence lurking around the corner or at the foot of the bed. The second is the incubus type, which manifests as a suffocating pressure on the chest, as if someone or something were sitting on top of us, preventing us from breathing. Unable to move or speak, the amygdala triggers an instinctive panic. Throughout the centuries, this phenomenon has given rise to countless myths in all cultures. For example, there's the story of the old witch who steals your breath or the modern Hatman, the man in the hat, while other beliefs attribute it to demons or invading spirits. However, there's nothing paranormal about them. It's just your gray matter projecting ancestral survival fears while your muscles remain in pause mode. There's another phenomenon that defies all logic and has fueled myths for centuries. Can you guess what we're going to talk about next? Sleepwalking. The activation of a body without an owner occurs during the deepest stages of sleep, the non-REM phase. In this state, a dissociation takes place. The cerebral cortex responsible for conscious thought and memory remains disconnected, but the motor system is activated. The result is an automaton capable of walking, opening doors, moving furniture, or even leaving the house. Although they walk with their eyes open, they don't process information in the same way. Their brain activates the visual and motor areas necessary to avoid a table or open a doorknob. But the recognition areas, the ones that would tell them that the person in front of them is their mother and not a shadow, are switched off. They see the world as a physical obstacle, not as a meaningful reality. And why are they able to move? Unlike what happens in sleep paralysis, here the muscle switch hasn't been turned off. It's not that the sleepwalker is doing in real life what they are dreaming, since in this deep phase there is hardly any dream activity, but rather that their brain is trapped in a biological limbo. To understand sleepwalking, we should imagine the brain as a house with many rooms. As we sleep, we turn off the lights in each room. In a brain with standard functioning, when we enter deep sleep, the lights for voluntary movement and consciousness turn off in the first few hours of the night. However, in a sleepwalker, the movement switch remains on or is accidentally activated, while the room of consciousness, the prefrontal cortex, remains dark. It's an intrusion of wakefulness into deep sleep. What causes sleepwalking? There isn't just one, but a combination of factors that push the brain into this state. Genetics is the most powerful factor. If both parents are sleepwalkers, their child has a 60% chance of being one as well. A predisposition to experience partial awakenings from non-REM sleep is inherited . Another important factor is sleep deprivation. The less we sleep, the deeper our recovery sleep is the next day. This dense sleep is the ideal breeding ground for sleep failure, causing the body to wake up without the mind even noticing. This phenomenon has a technical explanation: slow-wave sleep rebound. When we accumulate sleep debt, our brain tries to recover it by increasing the intensity and depth of non-REM sleep the following night. The denser and heavier this recovery sleep is, the harder it is for the brain to manage a smooth transition back to wakefulness, making it easier for the sleep-wake switch to flip while the rest of the house remains dark. Stress and fever can also cause sleepwalking because both conditions increase sleep fragmentation. Fever, in particular, alters brain chemistry in a way that facilitates these episodes, especially in children. And finally, we have to consider brain immaturity as a cause. This is why it's so common in childhood, affecting about 15% of children. Their sleep control systems are still developing, and it's normal for the switch to malfunction until the brain matures. If sleepwalking appears suddenly in adulthood without any history in childhood, it is a warning sign that should not be ignored. Sleepwalking can be a symptom of something disrupting deep sleep. For example, undiagnosed sleep apnea or a side effect of certain medications. In older adults, these episodes are often precursors to neurodegenerative disorders, so visiting a sleep clinic is highly recommended to try to determine the cause . Can sleepwalking be cured? In most cases, especially in children, it disappears on its own with age. It's not an illness, but a parasomnia, meaning an unwanted event that occurs during sleep. In any case, there are ways to manage it, and the best approach is sleep hygiene. Maintaining strict schedules and getting enough sleep significantly reduces episodes. In chronic cases, it's recommended to observe when the episode usually occurs and wake the person about 15 minutes earlier to break the deep sleep cycle and restart it. It's also recommended to install safety locks, remove sharp objects from the floor, or put up safety gates on stairs to ensure the sleepwalker's safety. Only in very serious cases, where the sleepwalker is in real danger or suffers violent episodes, can doctors prescribe low doses of benzodiazepines to suppress the deepest sleep phases where the phenomenon occurs. You've probably heard a thousand times that waking a sleepwalker is dangerous, that it could cause a heart attack or put them in a coma, but that's not true. What happens is that, being in such a deep sleep, if you wake them at that moment, they will feel disoriented, frightened, and could react aggressively out of pure instinct for self-defense. Therefore, the medical recommendation is neither to wake them nor to let them wander, as they could fall or hurt themselves, but rather to guide them gently back to bed. During this journey, you should speak softly in a low tone, using very short words like, "Come, follow me," or "Let's go." It would only be necessary to wake them if they are about to put themselves in real danger. Let's talk now about one of the most deeply rooted and debated customs in places like Spain and much of Latin America. Is the siesta an act of laziness or a biological necessity? This practice has often been stigmatized as a sign of indolence, but etymology and biology agree that it has a strong justification. History tells us that the term itself comes from the Latin phrase "hora sexta." In the Roman Empire's system of dividing time, the daylight period was segmented into 12 hours. The sixth hour corresponded to solar noon. At that moment, workers would interrupt their labors to escape the extreme heat, regain their strength, and avoid heatstroke. This custom took deep root in the Iberian Peninsula. Well, modern science has shown that the Romans were right when they decided to take a siesta for reasons that go beyond sociology. Chronobiology demonstrates that the siesta responds to our body's needs. Human circadian rhythms dictate that between 7 and 8 hours after waking up, our bodies experience a physiological drop in core temperature. This decrease is accompanied by a reduction in alertness and concentration. And pay attention to this because it's a fact that often causes confusion. This energy dip occurs regardless of the amount of food ingested; that is, it's not just the result of heavy digestion. We are programmed to seek a brief daytime rest. Perhaps some of you are wondering, "So why is it that when I've taken a 2-hour nap I usually wake up grumpy, disoriented, and feeling like I don't even know what year it is?" In a short nap, we remain in the light sleep phases, so our body is relaxed, but it's easy to wake up. In contrast, if we sleep for 2 hours, our brain has time to enter the slow-wave sleep phase, the deepest of all. If the alarm clock rings right at that point of no return, we experience a clinical phenomenon called sleep inertia. The brain needs time to reactivate all its cortical areas. And this forced awakening causes irritability, motor clumsiness, and confusion. That's why sometimes sleeping in at odd hours is worse than not sleeping at all. Sleep medicine specialists emphasize that a brief rest of about 20 to 30 minutes during this circadian window is enough to mitigate stress, enhance memory consolidation, and improve mood. All this without inducing that groggy feeling caused by excessive rest. Therefore, remember, the siesta is not a sign of cultural laziness. It is an intelligent adaptation to our own internal rhythms that today's long working hours try to suppress, committing yet another assault against our nature. At this point, the question is, what happens inside us when we finally manage to fall into a deep sleep? And why is it so vital to protect that moment? In recent years, between 2024 and 2026, advances in neuroscience have shed light on a striking biological process: the lymphatic system. This network of channels was discovered by Danish neuroscientist Mike Nethergar and is our brain's cleaning service. During the day, the intense activity of our neurons generates waste products such as beta-amyloid and tau proteins, which are associated with neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer's. When we enter the slow-wave sleep phase, the glial cells in the human brain shrink at a microscopic level, causing the space between them to expand by up to 60%. This contraction allows cerebrospinal fluid to flow like a tide through channels called aquaporin 4, washing the brain tissue and carrying toxins to the lymphatic system for final elimination by the liver. But what happens to your body if you don't get enough sleep? It's not just about having dark circles under your eyes or yawning at the office. At a physiological level, sleep deprivation is devastating for your body. Neuroscientist Matthew Walker has shown that without rest, the amygdala becomes up to 60% more reactive. This means we become irritable, impulsive, and lose the ability to regulate stress. Furthermore, in the long term, insufficient sleep prevents our brain from detoxifying, leading to an accumulation of metabolic waste that impairs our cognitive abilities. Added to this is hormonal chaos. If you don't sleep enough, your body reduces the production of leptin, the hormone that makes you feel full, and spikes levels of ghrelin, the hunger hormone. The result is that your primitive brain, feeling exhausted, goes into panic mode and drives you to seek quick energy, triggering uncontrollable cravings for sugars and carbohydrates. Lack of sleep is, in fact, one of the biggest risk factors for obesity in modern societies. And if we're talking about obstacles that prevent the deep brainwashing we mentioned, we have to mention an enemy that many doctors call the silent killer. Have you noticed that someone in your family sometimes snores and seems to run out of breath at certain times? This is due to a disorder called obstructive sleep apnea. This disorder occurs due to various factors, including obesity, anatomical factors such as enlarged tonsils or adenoids , and excessive muscle relaxation. The latter happens when the throat muscles relax too much during sleep, and the tissues collapse, blocking the passage of air to the lungs. In obstructive sleep apnea, the brain, upon detecting a lack of oxygen, panics and triggers micro-awakenings to force breathing. This can happen dozens of times an hour without the person being aware of it. The result is not only extreme fatigue the next day. In the long term, this continuous lack of oxygen increases the risk of developing hypertension, heart attacks, and strokes. Furthermore, by fragmenting sleep and preventing us from entering the slow-wave phase, apnea paralyzes the lymphatic system, and without nighttime cleansing, toxins accumulate and the risk of developing, for example, Alzheimer's disease increases. By the way, we know that something called mouth taping has become fashionable. It involves placing a small adhesive strip over the lips before sleeping to encourage nasal breathing. Although breathing through the nose is important, scientists warn that this technique can be dangerous if you suffer from undiagnosed sleep apnea, as it prevents your body from reacting to a lack of oxygen. It's best to consult an ear, nose, and throat (ENT) specialist. As we mentioned earlier, since the Industrial Revolution, we live in a society that never turns off the lights, so that currently around 20% of the working population in developed countries works rotating or night shifts. This is a large-scale biological experiment that science is analyzing with growing concern. Sleep medicine defines this phenomenon as a severe chronodisruption. By working when the body expects rest and eating when the body should be fasting, we cause a profound desynchronization between our central clock located in the brain and the peripheral clocks of our organs. Recent research shows that glucose metabolism becomes inefficient outside of daylight hours, significantly increasing the risk of developing type 2 diabetes and obesity. But there's something even more invisible and dangerous. The lymphatic system, that brain cleaning brigade we just discussed, doesn't function as effectively during daytime sleep. Night shift workers' rest is usually shorter and more fragmented, preventing the complete elimination of toxic waste from the brain. This has been linked to a more accelerated cognitive decline and a higher risk of developing neurodegenerative diseases in the long term. Fortunately, science also offers solutions to mitigate the damage. It has been shown that the impact is much less if shift rotation follows a clockwise direction, that is, going from morning to afternoon and from afternoon to night. This is because our circadian rhythm has a natural tendency to shift back. The body finds it much easier to adapt to going to bed later than to trying to sleep several hours earlier than usual. And even if your job isn't night shift or involves shifts, those of you who work daytime jobs from Monday to Friday aren't immune to sleep problems either. Because, let's face it, who has ever asked us this question? If I only sleep five hours during the week because of work, can I make up for lost sleep by sleeping in for 12 hours on Saturday and Sunday? The answer is no. Rest doesn't work like a bank account. You can't accumulate sleep debt and pay it off on the weekend. When we drastically alter our schedules on Saturdays and Sundays compared to our weekday routine, we cause what experts call social jet lag. Our brains become disoriented as if we've traveled to another continent, and falling asleep on Sunday night becomes impossible, perpetuating the cycle of exhaustion. The metabolic and cognitive damage from sleeping too little from Monday to Friday is already done and can't be erased by a lazy morning. In fact, science has just issued a very serious warning about irregular bedtimes. A study conducted by the University of Oulu in Finland and published in March 2016 in the journal BMC Cardiovascular Disorders concluded that constantly changing our bedtime and getting less than eight hours of sleep doubles our risk of suffering a heart attack or stroke compared to those who maintain a consistent daily routine. According to this study, which followed more than 3,000 adults for a decade, our cardiovascular system needs this routine. By going to bed at different times each night, we disrupt our circadian rhythm. This imbalance prevents the heart from having the rest and recovery periods it needs, subjecting it to continuous stress. Given this evolutionary context, the big question many of you are probably asking is, What if I suffer from chronic insomnia or think I have sleep apnea? Can my problem be fixed? Before discussing therapies, it's important to know that if you're not sleeping well, the first step should never be to look for home remedies online or self-medicate. The main action is to seek professional help, and the starting point for achieving this, accessible to almost everyone, is to make an appointment with your primary care physician or family doctor. This professional is key to conducting an initial evaluation, ruling out other illnesses, and referring you to the appropriate specialist: a pulmonologist, neurologist, ENT specialist, or neurophysiologist. And you'll likely end up in a sleep unit. In these hospital departments, doctors and experts in sleep disorders will be able to conduct a thorough study to rule out physical problems and develop a treatment plan. By the way, once you're in the office of these professionals, the first thing we must dispel is the idea that the solution always involves taking a pill to force the brain to surrender. Research from 2025, led by scientist Natalie Haugl, has issued a warning. The use of common sleeping pills like zolpidem can reduce the effectiveness of the brain's lymphatic system, its natural cleaning mechanism, by 30%. This means that drug-induced sleep doesn't always equate to restorative rest at the cellular level. They switch you off, yes, but they don't allow you to truly rest. Clinical science from 2026, supported by institutions like the American Academy of Sleep Medicine, explains that the first- line treatment shouldn't be a pill, but rather cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia, known as ICBT. They claim it's effective in 70 to 80% of cases, outperforming any medication in the long run. We're not talking about the typical basic advice like drinking a glass of milk or not having coffee in the afternoon. ICBT is neurobiological training that reconfigures your brain's connections. It's based on two main pillars. The first involves stimulus control. The goal is to break the toxic association your brain has created between your bed and the anxiety of not sleeping. The rule is strict. If you've been tossing and turning for 20 minutes, you must get up, leave the room, and engage in a relaxing activity in dim light until sleep overcomes you. Of course, no screens. We'll explain why later. It's very common to put televisions in bedrooms these days, but the bed should once again be a sanctuary exclusively for rest. Your brain needs to understand that this piece of furniture is synonymous with peace and tranquility. The second pillar of IBT is sleep restriction. It sounds contradictory, doesn't it? But the best way to cure insomnia is to spend less time in bed. By restricting the hours you spend lying down, you increase your biological sleep pressure. This consolidates your rest immediately, eliminating awakenings in the middle of the night, and little by little, guided by a therapist, you expand that window of sleep. Until very recently, the lack of specialized therapists posed a nearly insurmountable barrier to accessing these types of treatments. However, technology has helped democratize them in many places. In 2025, agencies like the US FDA approved digital TCCI platforms such as the Sleepy X program. Clinical trials have shown that these digital therapies reduce the time needed to fall asleep by 55%. And what about medicine? When behavioral therapy needs reinforcement, if the expert deems it appropriate, medications that have made an evolutionary leap in this field can be used. Aggressive sedatives like benzodiazepines are a thing of the past. These classic drugs work by enhancing an inhibitory neurotransmitter called GABA, which indiscriminately shuts down the brain. This artificial shutdown disrupts the natural architecture of rest and, as we saw earlier, blocks the lymphatic system, promoting the accumulation of brain waste. The major medical advance today, according to experts, is the so-called oroxine receptor antagonists, with innovative active ingredients such as lemborexant. Laurexine It's a neurotransmitter in our brain responsible for keeping us alert. Instead of drastically sedating the entire nervous system, these new drugs work by blocking this wakefulness switch. By turning off the alert signal, they allow natural sleep to flow on its own, without disrupting the deep sleep stages and without causing that chemical hangover or sluggishness the next morning. However, remember that all medications can have side effects. Knowing all this, how can we apply the wisdom of our ancestors and modern science? To improve our rest. We're going to give you eight practical tips based on modern chronobiology that can help you sleep better. First, restrict the use of your bed exclusively to sleep and intimacy. No laptops, answering emails, or looking at your phone once you're in bed. In fact, doctors recommend cutting off digital devices two hours before bedtime. We need darkness, and the blue light from screens tricks your brain and reduces melatonin production. By avoiding these habits, we prevent the brain from associating that place of rest with cognitive alertness, work stress, or bright light. We need to recapture the darkness of our Paleolithic ancestors to resynchronize our circadian rhythm. Second, try to go to bed at roughly the same time every day. This will help regulate your biological clock. Third, regular exercise is a great way to promote rest, but it's crucial to know when it helps us sleep and when it hinders us. Experts recommend avoiding vigorous exercise at least two or three hours before bedtime. The reason is that intense exertion triggers cortisol and raises internal temperature just when the brain needs it to start lowering to initiate sleep. Fourth, pay attention to the ambient temperature. Our brain needs the room to be cool, around 18 degrees Celsius. Why? Throughout our species' history, sunset has always been accompanied by a significant drop in temperature. Our primitive brain learned to use that nighttime chill as an unmistakable signal to secrete melatonin and shut down the body. That's why, to begin resting, your core body temperature needs to drop by about 1 degree Celsius. If the room is too warm, the body is unable to release its own heat, directly blocking access to the deep sleep phases, which is what happens to us in summer. Scientific consensus establishes that the ideal environment should be cool, around 18 degrees Celsius. Fifth, to help with this slight core hypothermia necessary for deep sleep, we must consider our diet. Hunter-gatherer tribes ate their main meal before sunset. Eat dinner at least two hours before bedtime. This ensures that your body's resources are concentrated on tissue repair and brain function, rather than on heavy digestion that raises the core body temperature and prevents the brain from truly switching off. Sixth, be mindful of stimulants. Caffeine has a half-life of about 6 hours, which means that after-lunch coffee can still be in your system at 10 p.m., blocking your adenosine receptors. It's recommended to avoid it at least 8 to 10 hours before bed, and above all, avoid alcohol. Although it might help you fall asleep quickly because it's a sedative, it actually fragments sleep, blocks the REM phase, and dehydrates the body, leaving you tired when you wake up. Seventh. If you ever wake up at 3 a.m. and can't fall back asleep immediately, try not to let anxiety get the better of you. Think of it as that ancestral "wake-up call" we talked about earlier. Instead of tossing and turning in frustration and spiking your cortisol, get up. Do a relaxing activity in dim light, no screens, and wait for sleep to return on its own. And the last, eighth piece of advice isn't for the night, but for waking up. We need to expose ourselves to sunlight for at least 30 minutes first thing in the morning. This acts as a trigger. This resets our circadian clock and abruptly halts the production of residual melatonin, signaling to the brain that the day has begun. One last piece of advice: don't become obsessed with the data provided by your smartwatches, which can tell you how well you sleep each night. There's a phenomenon called orthosomnia, which is the stress caused by trying to achieve the perfect sleep score. But sleep isn't a competition; it's a natural process that flows better when we stop trying to control it down to the last detail. Furthermore, while smartwatches are more or less reliable tools for monitoring sleep and wake times, they have limited accuracy, often with a 20 to 50% error rate in precisely distinguishing between deep and REM sleep stages. This is because they work by inferring data from movement and heart rate, not from actual brain activity, so they cannot replace a medical study in a sleep unit. As we've seen throughout history, sleep has shaped who we are. From those nights under the warmth of a fire on the savanna, through medieval shared beds, to the current insomnia epidemic, humankind has never stopped searching for ways to rest peacefully. Perhaps to sleep better in the future, we only need to look to our past and reconnect with the biology written in our genes. If I ask you to write "respect" in the comments, it's so that you remember this for the rest of your life, so that it's engraved in your heart. Respect isn't earned by showing your weaknesses, by exposing your vulnerability. Respect is earned by respecting yourself first. And when you give someone a gift, you never give a gift to submit.
